economic benefits of expanded C/Z's-T/A's would be a reduction in the number of interchanges and a reduction in the related costs now sustained, through the elimination of costs associated with extra travel and rehandling of materials. Improvements in service would result through more alternatives by shippers/carriers in planning pickups, deliveries and shipments. It is questionable that shippers would benefit servicewise by the simple access to a greater number of carriers. Studies made to date indicate that most shippers already have numerous choices of carriers and that rate/service competition is substantial.
There appears to be little question that many short-haul carriers would be affected by such an expansion. Many carriers have stated that they would lose from 20 to 70 percent of their volume and revenues as a result of expanded C/Z's-T/A's. For some carriers, these losses in volume/revenues would result primarily because of reductions in potential interchange freight in connection with line-haul carriers. Logic suggests with such new opportunity line-haul carriers will tend to explore these potential benefits. The same concerns relating to traditional discussions of lesser regulation would come into play in the consideration of expanded commercial zones and terminal areas. These concerns include the possibility of:
. reduced access to carrier financial markets
. reduced stability in carrier service
. increased difficulty in processing loss/damage/shortage claims
. reduced rate stability
. reduced overall carrier fitness
. reduced insurance stability
. less structural rate publication.
Such concerns could well be balanced against the possibility of:
. greater rate flexibility
. increased flexibility in operating response
. flexible insurance standards
